sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Learn about the studio behind Elle Woods' story.
sceneFacts.factHeader: MGM took a chance on this hit comedy

factBeats.text: MGM offered Robert Luketic the chance to direct Legally Blonde, which he eagerly accepted.
MGM was keen to sign up a film adaptation of Amanda Brown's novel, even though no publisher had expressed interest in the book.
With a budget of only $18 million, Legally Blonde made a sizable profit for MGM.

factBeats.text: When viewers first meet Elle Woods, she is wearing a "pink prints charming" look, complete with Barbie-style mules and a rhinestone heart.
The dress features a cloud print that enhances its fuchsia hue and adds personality to the outfit.
The outfit's silhouette is a classic wrap-dress style, popular in the early 2000s.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Elle's major was more common than you think.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Elle's fashion major had real-life roots.

factBeats.text: Elle's fashion merchandising major was considered an unconventional path for a law school applicant.
However, the author of the "Legally Blonde" novel, Amanda Brown, also majored in fashion when she applied to Stanford Law.
Similarly, screenwriter Karen McCullah Lutz minored in fashion merchandising in college.
Law schools often seek diverse majors, making Elle's unique background an asset rather than a hindrance.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: How did the actors prepare for sorority life?
sceneFacts.factHeader: Reese Witherspoon's "anthropological study" for sorority life

factBeats.text: Reese Witherspoon and Jessica Cauffiel prepared for their sorority roles by spending time with a real sorority.
They invited an entire sorority to dinner, offering to buy them free margaritas all night.
While the sorority girls "got tanked," Witherspoon and Cauffiel stayed sober and took notes.
Witherspoon described her time with the sorority girls as "an anthropological study."

Animal trainer Sue Chip had the good fortune to train and work with Moonie on both "Legally Blonde" films.

factBeats.text: The actual Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, was not used for most of the filming.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Paulette's storyline almost took a wild turn.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Paulette's iconic B-plot was a spontaneous invention

factBeats.text: Screenwriters Karen McCullah and Kirsten Smith wanted to give Jennifer Coolidge's character, Paulette, a significant secondary storyline.
Early ideas for Paulette's B-plot included a crime, such as the nail salon being robbed.
The writers found these crime plots "tonally weird" and instead decided to focus on Paulette's romantic life.
This led to the creation of the "Bend and Snap" scene, which Kirsten Smith spontaneously invented at a bar.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Where did Harvard Law's courtroom scenes really film?
sceneFacts.factHeader: This courtroom is a historic California landmark

factBeats.text: The courtroom scenes for "Legally Blonde" were filmed in part at the old Orange County Courthouse.
This impressive red sandstone building is located in downtown Santa Ana, California.
Courtroom No. 1 within the courthouse, beautifully restored to its original glory, is much prized by filmmakers.
The courthouse, which opened in 1901, is also listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
